title: Y-chromosomal Adam
blurb: Not the first man — the one whose Y chromosome is the only one with unbroken father-to-son descent to every living man. Everyone else's line died out.

title: A00
blurb: The deepest branch known, found in a handful of Mbo families in Cameroon. It splits off before the rest of humanity's paternal tree even begins.

title: A0-T
blurb: The stem carrying everyone who is not A00.

title: A0
blurb: Rare today, concentrated in western Central Africa.

title: A1
blurb: A trunk node — no living population is 'A1', it is simply where two branches part.

title: A1a
blurb: Carried today in Senegal, Guinea-Bissau and Mali.

title: A1b
blurb: The stem leading to almost every man alive.

title: A1b1
blurb: Associated with Khoisan-speaking populations of southern Africa.

title: BT
blurb: East Africa. From here the tree becomes the story of everyone.

title: B
blurb: Common among Central African rainforest hunter-gatherer groups and parts of the Sahel.

title: CT
blurb: Every man outside Africa, and most inside it, descends from this node. The out-of-Africa bottleneck sits just after it.

title: DE
blurb: A node that immediately splits into an African branch and an Asian one — the clearest single fork in the exit story.

title: E
blurb: Now the majority lineage across Africa. Whether E arose in Africa or arose in the Near East and came back is genuinely unsettled.

title: E1b1a
blurb: West Africa. The lineage that would later ride the Bantu expansion across a continent.

title: E1b1a (Bantu expansion)
blurb: In roughly two thousand years, farming communities carried this lineage from West Africa to the southern tip of the continent — the fastest large-scale expansion in African prehistory.

title: E1b1b
blurb: Northeast Africa, later spreading along both shores of the Mediterranean.

title: E1b1b (Mediterranean)
blurb: North Africa and the Mediterranean rim; carried into Europe repeatedly.

title: D
blurb: An Asian lineage with a strange, broken distribution — Tibet, Japan and the Andaman Islands, and almost nowhere between.

title: D (Andamanese)
blurb: Isolated on the Andaman Islands for tens of thousands of years.

title: D1a (Tibet)
blurb: One of the two dominant paternal lineages on the Tibetan plateau.

title: D1b (Japan)
blurb: The Jōmon lineage — carried by Japan's pre-agricultural population and still around a third of Japanese men today.

title: CF
blurb: The branch that leaves Africa and becomes nearly everyone in Eurasia, Oceania and the Americas.

title: C
blurb: An early traveller. C turns up at the far ends of the human range — Australia, Mongolia, and among the first Americans.

title: C1b2 (Sahul)
blurb: Among the first Australians. They crossed open water to get there, at least 65,000 years ago by the archaeology.

title: C2 (Northeast Asia)
blurb: Siberia and Mongolia.

title: C2 (steppe)
blurb: The dominant paternal lineage of the eastern steppe, later spread hard by Mongol expansion.

title: F
blurb: More than nine in ten men outside Africa descend from F. A single node, a single window of time.

title: GHIJK
blurb: The fan-out. Within a few thousand years this node produces most of the lineages of Eurasia.

title: G
blurb: The Caucasus and eastern Anatolia.

title: G2a
blurb: Anatolia, on the eve of farming.

title: G2a (Neolithic Europe)
blurb: The signature lineage of Europe's first farmers. Ötzi the Iceman carried it. It is rare in Europe now — later migrations largely replaced it.

title: HIJK
blurb: Stem.

title: H
blurb: South Asia, deeply rooted and still common there.

title: H1
blurb: Widespread across the Indian subcontinent.

title: IJK
blurb: Stem.

title: IJ
blurb: The Near Eastern fork: one branch becomes European, the other stays and becomes Levantine and Arabian.

title: I
blurb: Europe's own deep lineage — the paternal line of the continent's Ice Age hunter-gatherers.

title: I2
blurb: Present in European foragers before farming arrived.

title: I2a
blurb: Survives best in the Balkans and the Dinaric Alps.

title: I1
blurb: Scandinavia. A young, explosive expansion from a very small founding group.

title: J
blurb: The Fertile Crescent lineage.

title: J1
blurb: The Levant and Arabia.

title: J1 (Arabia)
blurb: Dominant across the Arabian peninsula today.

title: J2
blurb: The Zagros and Anatolia — herders and, later, the farming societies of the northern Fertile Crescent.

title: J2 (Mediterranean)
blurb: Carried west along the Mediterranean with farming and, much later, with Greek and Phoenician settlement.

title: K
blurb: Stem — and the ancestor of most of Asia, Oceania and the Americas.

title: L · T
blurb: A quiet branch: South Asia, the Iranian plateau, and pockets around the Mediterranean.

title: L
blurb: Pakistan and western India.

title: K2
blurb: Southeast Asia. The last common ancestor of East Asians, Papuans, Siberians and Native Americans.

title: NO
blurb: The East Asian stem.

title: N
blurb: Turns north and west, and ends up ringing the Arctic.

title: N1c (Siberia)
blurb: A sweep across the Siberian taiga, west along the forest belt.

title: N1c (Finland & Baltic)
blurb: More than half of Finnish men carry a lineage whose recent ancestors lived in Siberia.

title: O
blurb: The dominant paternal lineage of East and Southeast Asia — carried by roughly a fifth of all men alive.

title: O2
blurb: North China.

title: O2 (millet farmers)
blurb: Rice and millet farming turned three founding lineages into hundreds of millions of descendants.

title: O1
blurb: South China coast.

title: O1 (Taiwan)
blurb: The launch point of the Austronesian expansion.

title: O1 (Remote Oceania)
blurb: From Taiwan to Polynesia: the longest open-ocean colonisation in prehistory, ending in Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.

title: K2b
blurb: Stem.

title: M · S (Papua)
blurb: New Guinea and Island Melanesia, isolated for tens of thousands of years.

title: P
blurb: Central Asia. From here, two of the great expansions.

title: Q
blurb: South Siberia.

title: Q-M3 (Beringia)
blurb: A small population sat isolated on the Bering land bridge for thousands of years — long enough to accumulate its own mutations — before the ice opened.

title: Q-M3 (North America)
blurb: Once the route opened, the continent filled fast.

title: Q-M3 (South America)
blurb: From Alaska to Patagonia in perhaps 1,500 years — the fastest continental colonisation in the human record.

title: R
blurb: Central Asia. Rare for twenty thousand years, then suddenly everywhere.

title: R1a
blurb: The eastern steppe branch.

title: R1a-M417
blurb: The Pontic-Caspian steppe, at the moment horses and wheels change what distance means.

title: R1a (Corded Ware)
blurb: North and east across Europe.

title: R1a (South Asia)
blurb: The same steppe lineage turns up in northern India — one of the most contested findings in the field.

title: R1b
blurb: The western steppe branch.

title: R1b-M269
blurb: The Yamnaya world: mobile pastoralists on the Pontic-Caspian grassland.

title: R1b (Bell Beaker)
blurb: Within a few centuries this lineage replaces most of the existing paternal ancestry of Britain. The pots travelled; so, it turns out, did the people.

title: R1b (Atlantic façade)
blurb: Now the most common paternal lineage in western Europe — over 80% of men in Ireland and the Basque country.
